en: The First Section of the Nārāyaṇapūrvatāpinī Upaniṣad. Then Sanatkumāra questioned the venerable Brahmā: "What is the nature of the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa? He explained: "Now, he who is indeed Nārāyaṇa is the Blessed One, the bliss of the Supreme Brahman. By knowing this, one becomes liberated while living; one becomes the supreme reality whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss. The eight-syllabled mantra is the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrti). Its first form is the form of the earth; the second is water; the third is fire."
The fourth becomes wind; the fifth becomes space; the sixth becomes the moon; the seventh becomes the sun; the eighth is the sacrificer.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the moon,
the sun, and the Puruṣa— these are proclaimed as the eight forms.

Through the contemplation and meditation upon the syllables *a*, *u*, *ma*, *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, along with their synthesis (*anusandhāna*), there arise the eightfold aspects of the eight-syllabled mantra. The syllable *a* is Sadyojāta; *u* is Vāmadeva; *ma* is Aghora; *nāda* is Tatpuruṣa; *bindu* is Īśāna; *kalā* is Vyāpaka; *anusandhāna* is Nitya; and the nature of meditation (*dhyāna*) is Brahman. Thus, the eight-syllabled mantra is all-pervading.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme knowledge.
[I bow to] Nārāyaṇa, the Great Person, the universe, the self, and the imperishable.
Nārāyaṇa, the supreme, abides both within and without all that;
he is the thousand-headed god, the imperishable, the highest state.
Nārāyaṇa, Śiva, the peaceful one, who is the object of all Vedāntas; the performer of the fivefold cosmic acts— creation, sustenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace— the healthy Nārāyaṇa.
Thus ends the first section in the *Nārāyaṇapūrvatāpinī* of the *Atharvaṇarahasya*.

The second section: The Lord Brahmā spoke; he expounded the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa. The ten mantras of Śrīman-Nārāyaṇa are now told. "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya"—this is the eight-syllabled mantra. That indeed is the king of mantras. This is the *tāraka* (the deliverer) of Nārāyaṇa. That alone is to be worshipped. Thus spoke the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is the Supreme Brahman expressed by the word Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Great Māyā, Nature (*prakṛti*), and Lakṣmī, the sole mother of all.

She becomes the divine splendor of the gods; she becomes the perfected splendor of the Siddhas; she becomes the splendor of liberation for those seeking release; she becomes the splendor of yoga for yogins; she becomes the intellect of discernment for sages; she becomes the royal splendor of kings. She is Sarasvatī in the form of emanation; she is Mahālakṣmī in the form of maintenance; she is Rudrāṇī in the form of withdrawal; she is Pārvatī as the cause of concealment; she is Umā in the form of grace.
The Supreme Goddess manifests in the form of the fivefold acts. "Obeisance to Śrī Mahālakṣmī" is the seven-syllabled mantra.
The Great Goddess Mahālakṣmī, who bestows great good fortune upon all beings,
is the sole enchantress of all the worlds.
She is the eternal bestower of sovereignty, the embodiment of all the Vedas;
she is the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), the Mother of the World, and the giver of liberation to the sages. She grants wisdom to the wise, is Truth itself, and is the destroyer of the Dānavas.

Thus Mahālakṣmī is the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*). That Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa is the very essence of the Supreme Brahman, the object of all the Upaniṣads, and consists of the eternally pure, enlightened, and supreme Brahman-bliss. Therefore, he is indeed called Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa; so said the Blessed One. He who knows thus—this is the Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the second section in the Nārāyaṇapūrvatāpinī of the Atharvaṇarahasya.
The third section begins.

The venerable Brahmā said: "What is the mantra of Nārāyaṇa like? 'Oṃ, we know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva; may that Viṣṇu inspire us'—this is the Gāyatrī. 'Viṣṇu strode through this [universe]; in three places he planted his step; his footstep is gathered in the dust' and 'From where Viṣṇu strode with the seven abodes of the earth, from there let the gods be ours'—by these two mantras, Nārāyaṇa is set forth."

"He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Hari, he is Indra; he is the Imperishable, the Supreme Self-ruler. Thus the five-syllabled mantra *nārāyaṇāya* arises. The six-syllabled *oṃ namo viṣṇave* is known. *Namo nārāyaṇāya* becomes seven syllables. *Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya* is proclaimed as twelve syllables. *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namo nārāyaṇāya svāhā*. This must not be given to anyone whatsoever.
One may give away a son, one may give away one's head, but the sixteen-syllabled [mantra] must not be given.
One should not speak it to just anyone, but one should speak it only to a disciple.
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva; svāhā!
Salutations to you, the illustrious Mahāviṣṇu, and to Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to Govinda, to Rudra, and to Hari who is the form of Brahman.
O Nārāyaṇa, O Mahāviṣṇu, O Śrīdhara, O Ananta, O Keśava!
O Vāsudeva, O Lord of the World, O Hṛṣīkeśa, salutations, salutations!
Thus the two *anuṣṭubh* verses have been explained as a mantra. Now we shall explain the *mālā-mantra*. The Blessed Lord Brahmā said: "He who knows thus"—this is the Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the third section in the *Nārāyaṇapūrvatāpinī* of the *Atharvaṇarahasya*.

The fourth section: The venerable Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke and explained the *Gāyatrī*: "May we know Govinda; may we meditate upon Vāsudeva; may that Nārāyaṇa inspire us. "May we know Kāmadeva; may we meditate upon the one with the flower-arrows; may that Anaṅga inspire us. "May we know the Great Goddess; may we meditate upon the consort of Viṣṇu; may that Lakṣmī inspire us. "I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who measured out the earthly realms."

"He who propped up the highest dwelling place, strode out across it in three steps, the wide-striding one. "Three times this god strode across this earth, which possesses a hundred splendors, by means of his greatness. May Viṣṇu be present, he who is more powerful than the powerful; for the name of this steadfast one is formidable.
"Where the wise have fashioned speech with their mind, purifying it like grain through a sieve—there friends recognize their friendships; upon their speech a blessed mark is set."

"Vishnu is praised for his heroic power: like a terrifying beast that roams and dwells in the mountains, in whose three wide strides all worlds abide. "He who hears him hears in vain; for he does not know the path of righteous action. "Friends endowed with eyes and ears have become unequal in their mental grasp regarding living beings. Therefore, he who knows Lakshmi-Narayana—the seed of all and the abode of all beings—becomes a wise man.

Liberation is attained by lay practitioners (*upāsakas*). He becomes one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). The Blessed One spoke thus, explaining the method of worship (*upāsanavidhi*): Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*); the *gāyatrī* is said to be the meter (*chandas*); the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self, is the deity (*devatā*); the syllable *praṇava* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); "namas" is said to be the power (*śakti*); and "Nārāyaṇa" is the pin (*kīlaka*).
Then follows the application to virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation, as well as the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

For Maholkā, Vīrolkā, Vṛddholkā, Pṛthūlkā, Vidyulkā, and Jvaladulkā, the ritual assignments of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are performed, ending with the words *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*. [The deity is visualized] resembling a dark blue cloud and clothed in yellow silk garments.
Wearing a crown and earrings, his chest was illuminated by the Kaustubha gem.
He bears the conch, the discus, the mace, and the sword, wears a garland of forest flowers,
and has his body half-merged in a close embrace by Mahālakṣmī on his left side.
Having meditated upon the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is served by Sanaka and others, praised by the great sages, and always contemplated by Brahmā and the rest;
With body, mind, and speech, the wise one should recollect and chant [the mantra];
by merely chanting it ten thousand times, one becomes the bestower of all knowledge.
One should recite [the mantra] exactly one hundred thousand times, and then the mantra becomes one's own essential nature;
beyond that, one should always meditate upon Hari as Nārāyaṇa manifest.
The Blessed One said: "He who knows thus. Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the fourth section in the Nārāyaṇapūrvatāpinīya of the Atharvaṇa-rahasya.
Now begins the fifth section:
The Blessed Lord Brahmā said, "The incarnation consisting of ten digits (kalās) is now described."
Jarā, Pālinikā, Śānti, Īśvarī, Ratikāmikā,
Varadā, Hlādinī, and Prīti— these are the ten digits (kalās) of Hari.

From Nārāyaṇa, incarnations arise in the form of mantras: *Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya svāhā*. Thus, there is this great ten-syllable mantra. Among them, the first is the Fish incarnation (*matsyāvatāra*); the second is the Tortoise (*kūrma*); the third is the Boar (*varāha*); the fourth is the Man-lion (*nṛsiṃha*); the fifth is the Dwarf (*vāmana*); the sixth is Jamadagni; the seventh is Rāmacandra; the eighth is Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); the ninth is the Buddha incarnation; and the tenth is Kalki Janārdana.
Oṃ, salutations to the Fish Incarnation. Salutations to the Glorious Tortoise Incarnation. Hrīṃ, salutations to the Boar Incarnation. Huṃ, salutations to the Man-Lion Incarnation.

*Sauḥ*, obeisance to the Vāmana incarnation; *Aiṃ*, obeisance to the Paraśurāma incarnation; *Glauṃ*, obeisance to Rāmacandra; *Klīṃ*, obeisance to Kṛṣṇa; *Blūṃ*, obeisance to the Buddha incarnation; *Saḥ*, obeisance to the Kalki incarnation. From this, Prajāpati is born; from him, Nārāyaṇa is born; Brahmā is born. From the presence of Brahmā, the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their subtle counterparts (*tanmātra*) are born. The organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*), mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), consciousness (*citta*), and ego (*ahaṃkāra*) are born.

Prakṛti is born. Nārāyaṇa consists of twenty-four principles (*tattvas*). That which consists of twenty-five principles is the state of Puruṣa; he is the Supreme Brahman. Śiva is Nārāyaṇa. Indra is Nārāyaṇa. The quarters are Nārāyaṇa. Above is Nārāyaṇa. Within is Nārāyaṇa. Indeed, all this is Nārāyaṇa, who is Brahman. From that Nārāyaṇa, all the great elements (*mahābhūtas*)—those born from eggs, from sweat, from sprouts, from a womb, and those born of the mind—are produced.
There is one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form;
one unborn male, indeed, lies beside her, enjoying her, while another unborn male abandons her once her enjoyment has been experienced.

Those born from eggs are born in all forms of birds; those born from sweat are worms, insects, and the like; those born from sprouts are trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth; those born from a womb are humans, domestic animals, wild beasts, and the like; those born from the mind are Nārada and all the other sages; Nārāyaṇa is the self of both the stationary and the moving; the eight Vasus are Nārāyaṇa; the eleven Rudras are Nārāyaṇa; and from Nārāyaṇa come the twelve Ādityas.

All the gods, ṛṣis, and munis, as well as the siddhas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas—all are Nārāyaṇa. This entire universe is indeed Nārāyaṇa. Lakṣmī is known as the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti). The one reality is the eternal Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa himself is designated as the Supreme Brahman.
Existence, consciousness, and bliss are eternally conceived within Viṣṇu, who is eternal;
his various forms are like bracelets and other ornaments fashioned from gold.

"There are four measured steps of speech; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth step of speech, humans speak. They say that Sarasvatī is fourfold, consisting of the forms *parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*. Among these, *vaikharī* is praised in all branches of knowledge.
The auxiliary sciences, the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā,
the extensive Nyāya, the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and the science of mantras—
these eighteen branches of knowledge are said to have been established by Nārāyaṇa.

His very breath is the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, and the Atharvangiras. The purport of all the Vedas and Upanishads is indeed upon Narayana, the Supreme Brahman. The Blessed One said: "He who knows thus. Thus ends the Upanishad.
Thus ends the fifth section in the *Nārāyaṇapūrvatāpinī* of the *Atharvaṇarahasya*.

The sixth section: The Blessed Lord Brahmā spoke; he taught the worship of the enclosure of mantras for the *Nārāyaṇayantra*. First is a triangle. Second is a hexagon. Third is a circle with eight petals. Fourth is one with twelve petals. Fifth is one with sixteen petals. Sixth is one with twenty-four [petals]. Seventh is one with thirty-two [petals]. Eighth is the outer square (*bhūpura*). In this manner, one should draw the yantra.

In the center, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is worshipped; the enclosure of the power of projection (vikṣepa-śakti), the deities of the triangle of power (śakti-trikoṇa) such as Śakti and Prabhā, and the six corners (ṣaṭkoṇa) where Vṛddholkā and others are to be worshipped. The powers of the hexagon (ṣaṭkoṇa-śaktayaḥ) are: omniscience, satisfaction, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, permanence, and infinite imperishability. On the eight petals are Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatsujāta, Sanatkumāra, Sanātana, Nārada, Tumburu, Samanta, and others.

Vasiṣṭha, Vālakhilya, Viśvāmitra, Kaśyapa, Atri, Bharadvāja, Aṅgīrasa, Jāmadagni, Gautama, Agastya, Jābāli, and Kapila are the twelve petals. Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nārasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, Paraśurāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki, along with Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna, and Parameśvara, are the sixteen petals.

The twenty-four petals represent Śaṅkha, Cakra, Gadā, Padma, Khaḍga, Śrīvatsa, Kaustubha, Vanamālā, and so forth; the crown, earrings, armlets, necklaces, bracelets, the bow Śārṅga, arrows, the sword Nandaka, the lotus, the flute, the peacock feather, Śeṣa, Ananta, Garuḍa, Viṣvaksena, and Brahmā, following the sequence of the twenty-four [incarnations] beginning with Keśava. The thirty-two petals represent Hari, Śrīkṛṣṇa, Mukunda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Dhāmaka, Śaṅkhavarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratīka.

Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, Supratīka, and Ākṣa are the deities of the four corners. "Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa"—thus the worship of the deities of the enclosure known by the eight-syllable mantra should be performed. The Blessed One said: "Whoever knows thus. This is the Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the sixth section in the Nārāyaṇapūrvatāpinīya within the Atharvaṇarahasya;
thus the Nārāyaṇapūrvatāpinī Upaniṣad is complete.
